title: Sana and the Gigantic Goulash Spill
markdown:
The air in Madam Periwinkle’s School for Aspiring Sorcerers smelled of old parchment and burnt sugar, which was usually as comforting as a biscuit. Today it also held a whiff of singed eyebrows and overripe cheese. That last note was mostly Sana. Her fingers were always smudged with ink, a bright map of spells that had not quite sat still.

Across the common room sat Gulliver, a gargoyle who polished his wings before breakfast. Some creatures have their priorities neatly folded. He worked a tiny cloth over one stone ear with the concentration of a jeweller, as if a dull patch might offend the furniture.

Sana’s desk was less a desk than a monument to lively mess. Potions shimmered or sat sadly flat on a stack of spellbooks opened at wildly unlikely angles. A lonely sock often peeked from under scrolls, its mate off on some private errand. In a sunlit corner Gulliver’s stone gleamed. He had watched buildings for centuries and preferred not to be surprised. Sana’s homework quill, which had a mischievous streak a mile wide, was newer trouble. It had a habit of writing tomorrow’s mishaps before anyone had the decency to cause them.

One Tuesday, Sana tried a levitation charm. Her teacup hovered a disappointing three inches too low. The quill shuddered, then scratched, far too loud for a feather:

Tomorrow: a Gigantic Goulash Spill threatens to engulf the Great Library.

Sana blinked. “Goulash? It isn’t even lunchtime.”

A shiver ran down her spine that had nothing to do with the window.

She wrung her ink-stained hands. “We have to stop it.”

Gulliver paused in buffing a small imperfection on his left ear. “Indeed,” he said, voice like pebbles in a quiet stream. “Panicking makes things messy. Perhaps we should learn what sort of spill it is. A potion is one thing. A philosophy is another.”

Sana stopped wringing. Gulliver was right, as he often was. Investigation, then. Prevent the spill. That was the work.

He did not rush her. He asked sensible questions and reminded her, by simply sitting there all polished and possible, that she had cleverness even when she misplaced it. Sana’s spark. Gulliver’s stillness.

The quill added a tiny footnote: Beware the Slippery Socks.

Sana checked her own feet, which were thankfully sockless, and pictured a professor skating down a corridor. Gulliver peered at a smudge she had missed.

“The ink is hasty,” he said. “Perhaps something else is slippery, not necessarily toes.”

They tiptoed the polished halls. Sana peered under benches and into the cloakroom, where a single striped sock lay innocent as a cat. No slicks. No mystery grease. Only floor wax, gleaming and ordinary. Near the pasture fence they found sheep, fluffy and unstartled, peering at the school as if considering enrolment. The quill had also mentioned a flock and considerable commotion.

“They’re not startled yet,” Gulliver observed. “We might keep it that way.”

So they did: no slammed doors, no practice thunderclaps from the weather courtyard, a long spell of clover and calm. Sana even walked the long way round so her boots would not clap. The sheep remained mere sheep. Late sun laid gold along their backs. Sana’s shoulders lowered a fraction.

Then the quill wrote: Wobbly Jelly Delivery arrives, much to everyone’s dismay.

They found the cart by the kitchens, lumbering with an unnerving wobble, stacked with enormous bowls of plum-purple jelly that trembled like nervous royalty. A kitchen lad had already begun to look dismayed in advance. Sana whispered a barely-there charm. The cart steadied. The bowls settled. The jelly wobbled only as jelly should, which is to say a little, and on purpose.

“We’re getting closer,” she whispered. Hope tasted like sugar on the air. “We’re actually doing it.”

For a moment she believed the library was saved: no slick disaster, no woolly riot, no jelly catastrophe. Then the quill gave a violent shudder.

The Goulash Spill is not averted, but merely redirected. It heads for the most precious thing of all.

Ink seemed to hurry. Soup Splash. Broth Brouhaha. Stew Situation. Sana and Gulliver darted corridors, peered into classrooms, and once intercepted a gravy boat that had no business on a windowsill. Always they were a step behind a word. The easy wins had only moved the mess. The Great Library — centuries of spells, scrolls, whispered secrets — sat at the far end of the worry like a held book, its oak doors still shut, which somehow made the threat more rude.

They stood in the main hall. The quill’s latest line pulsed: Goulash arrives with his bubbling cauldron.

Sana’s eyes snagged on the capital G.

“It isn’t a spill of goulash,” she said, voice thin. “It’s a spill caused by someone named Goulash. And his cauldron is coming here.”

Gulliver’s stony gaze stayed on the fading ink. “And it heads for the library.”

The quill confirmed it, one last shudder: Library in peril.

Sana slumped on a bench. Her inky fingers went limp. The thought of irreplaceable pages under bubbling stew made her feel like a very small boat. “We can’t stop him. It’s too big. Too Goulash-y.”

Gulliver set a surprisingly warm stone hand on her shoulder.

“Sana. The sheep. The jelly. We found ways. A clever distraction is kinder than a collision, especially with a man and a cauldron.” He nodded toward a forgotten corner where a student had left a harmless shimmer of goo that smelled faintly of strawberries. “Perhaps a little goo could be our friend.”

They mixed extra-gooey slime, pink as a wobbly raspberry, completely harmless, practically begging to be poked. A gruff voice bellowed down the corridor.

“Out of my way. Goulash coming through with the finest bubbling broth.”

They waited by the library doors. Just as a portly man with a steaming cauldron strapped to his back approached, Sana tossed the strawberry slime into his path.

Mr Goulash yelped. He stumbled. The cauldron lurched. Thick red soup sloshed — and landed, with a satisfying sploosh, on the waiting goo, which swallowed most of the drama in a sticky hug.

“Blast this goo,” he grumbled, distracted and slightly jammy. He decided, then and there, that sitting in the hallway to eat his soup, far from tempting books, was the wiser course.

Later, the school smelled of strawberries and a very mild, not-so-gigantic goulash. Sana and Gulliver sat in the dry library among the very shelves they had kept unsouped, sharing chamomile that spread through them like a contented sigh. Dust motes turned in the last of the afternoon. No parchment had learned to swim. The homework quill lay on Sana’s desk looking almost apologetic, its mischief dimmed. Sana’s fingers were still faintly inky. Her heart felt clean and quiet. Gulliver gave a small nod, and a rare smile found his stony face. He buffed his wing once, out of habit, as if even victory deserved a polish. The common room would be messy again tomorrow. The teacup would hover too low. For now the books stayed books, the sock could keep its adventure, and that was quite enough for one Tuesday.
characters: Sana (the ink-stained spell student), Gulliver (a polite gargoyle)
